component_records.title: Project management, governance and weekly reporting
component_records.description: A dedicated project manager plus named technical staff are assigned from award, with a personnel management plan identifying roles, hours of availability and escalation paths. The team holds weekly meetings that review progress, budget and timeline against a baseline schedule, with written status reports and a risk/issue log. The plan demonstrates the team's understanding of the City's auditing and reporting requirements and sets out how those requirements drive configuration, testing and acceptance. The schedule is built backwards from a July 1, 2026 go-live so that the new fiscal year opens on the new system, with a task sequence and milestones the City can hold the vendor to. Complete support for implementation and for ongoing services across all supplied applications is scoped as a single accountable engagement rather than a hand-off between phases.

component_records.title: Hosted accounting and financial reporting platform
component_records.description: A cloud-hosted accounting and financial reporting system is supplied, implemented and licensed for the City, covering the functional areas the City runs today: Accounts Payable with 1099 filing, purchasing requisitions and purchase orders with approvals; Accounts Receivable; General Ledger; Payroll; Utility Billing; and Business Licensing. Transactions are captured systematically at source with workflow and approval controls, and budgeting and forecasting are configured so the City can build, amend and compare budgets within the same system. Reporting and data analysis are delivered through a report library plus an ad hoc analysis tool so staff can produce decision-support information without vendor involvement. Every transaction carries an audit trail and supporting documentation is retained and retrievable, giving auditable records for future reference and for the City's auditors.

component_records.title: Licensing, account structure and solution design
component_records.description: The response identifies the license types offered at each level of use — named user, concurrent and read-only/reporting roles — and maps the City's five current users onto those levels with headroom for growth. It describes account number customisation in detail: segment structure, length, fund/function/object dimensions, validation rules and how the chart of accounts can be extended without re-implementation. The team recommends an account structure designed for auditable reporting, showing how segments roll up into the City's financial statements and how the structure supports fund accounting and audit sampling. Where any requirement is met by an additional application or a third-party vendor rather than the core platform, the response names the application, the vendor, the point in the workflow where it is used and the cost of including it.

component_records.title: Data migration and transition with minimal downtime
component_records.description: The prior five years of financial history are imported into the new system so that comparative reporting and audit look-back are available from day one. Migration covers master files (vendors, customers, employees, chart of accounts, utility accounts, licences) and historical transactions, with a documented extract from the City's current system, trial conversions, reconciliation to control totals and City sign-off before cutover. The team works directly with the City's Accounting and IT staff on a cutover plan — parallel running where useful, off-hours loading, and a rollback position — to minimise disruption and downtime during the transition. Financial report writing support is provided so the City's own statements and management reports are rebuilt and validated in the new system before go-live.

component_records.title: Training and change management
component_records.description: Power users in Accounting receive personalised, role-based training plus a written manual tailored to the City's configured system, so a small team can administer the platform day to day. All staff receive at least one recorded training session and a general manual, retained by the City for onboarding and refresher use. Training is offered in person, virtually and as standard recordings, and the response states which format applies at each license level so the City can choose. A short change-management plan covers communication, cutover-week floor support and a post-go-live refresher, sized for an 11-person organisation.

component_records.title: Ongoing support, updates and annual e-filing
component_records.description: Support is provided during implementation and continues through each annual contract renewal, with a named account manager and defined support levels for both implementation and recurring service. A help desk and ticketing system logs every request, assigns priority against agreed severity definitions and reports on response and resolution performance. Automated software updates are applied and communicated in advance, with release notes and change summaries so the City knows what has changed and when. The team supports the City's annual e-filing obligations, including 1099 and W-2 preparation and submission, and provides support for the first 12 months after implementation as a priced, included element of the proposal.

component_records.title: Price proposal and cost transparency
component_records.description: The price proposal states a total price for all services and deliverables, a total reimbursable expenses cap, and a total price proposal amount, presented so the relationship between the three is explicit. The implementation fee and recurring fees are broken out in detail, license fees are shown separately by license type and count, and support fees are split between implementation-period and post-implementation costs. The total price is the total cost to the City to perform all services requested, including materials, supplies and travel, with any reimbursable expenses capped rather than open-ended. Costs for any additional applications or third-party vendors identified in the solution are estimated and shown as a separate line.

component_records.title: Data protection and secure access controls
component_records.description: A data-protection pack documents the measures protecting the City's financial data: encryption in transit and at rest, segregated tenant hosting, backup and recovery objectives, retention and disposal, and incident response with breach notification. It documents the secure access controls in place — role-based permissions, least-privilege administration, multi-factor authentication, session controls, audit logging of user activity and periodic access reviews — and maps each control to the system components in scope. The pack is delivered as a narrative with supporting policy extracts and architecture diagrams so the City can assess it without a prescribed framework being named in the RFP.

component_records.title: Contract, compliance and certification obligations
component_records.description: A compliance register tracks every contractual obligation and evidences it in the submission. The response accepts that all RFP terms are enforceable as contract conditions under the General Contract Terms and Conditions, and that "shall", "must" and "requirements" create binding obligations, with no additional or modified terms submitted. A no-contact protocol binds the bid team, representatives, subcontractors and suppliers from submission to award, with a single named point of contact and an internal rule that any breach is reported immediately and may disqualify the bid. The bid team bears all proposal and interview costs with no claim on the City, and the price proposal is treated as final and not subject to alteration during clarification. Attachment D certification of financial condition is signed by an authorised officer, and the firm commits to notify the City within 30 days and the Contract Lead within 15 days of any material change to the certification, applying the shorter period to satisfy both. Attachment E proof of insurance for workers compensation and commercial general liability is attached, and Attachment C discloses whether any work is performed outside the United States, listing locations and corporate structure, with a written undertaking to notify the City of any relocation of personnel abroad.

component_records.title: Bid process, demonstration and references
component_records.description: A bid-process plan governs the submission itself: written questions are submitted to the City by the July 31, 2025 deadline, covering the standard contract terms, the Attachment F and G requirements, the reimbursable-expense cap basis and the offshoring disclosure, so that every ambiguity is resolved through the City's published answers before proposals are due. The response outlines virtual demonstration availability, including a scripted walkthrough of the modules the City uses and a live session for City staff, and offers at least one local referral able to attend an in-person demonstration. It commits the firm to virtual finalist interviews on September 25, 2025 if the City requires them, with the named implementation team present. Three or more references for similar municipal accounting implementations are supplied with client name, scope, performance dates, contact name, phone and valid email addresses, and the firm's qualifications, key personnel and subcontractor summaries are included.

items.text: The City of Colfax, California issued this RFP on July 1, 2025 for accounting and financial reporting software.

Colfax is a small Sierra Nevada foothills city in Placer County with a population just under 2,000, annual budgeted revenues of $6 million, 11 full-time employees (one position vacant) plus 1 part-time/seasonal/contract employee, and a June 30 fiscal-year end.

The City currently runs Fund Balance fund accounting software from Tyler Technologies with modules for Accounts Payable (including 1099 filing, purchasing requisitions, and purchase orders with approvals), Accounts Receivable, General Ledger, Payroll, Utility Billing, and Business Licensing, and has five users.

The City wants a single streamlined package that captures financial transactions systematically and efficiently, including budgeting and forecasting, reporting and data analysis for decision-making, and auditable records and documentation.
The City wants dedicated technical support both during implementation and across annual contract renewals, indicating an ongoing service relationship rather than a one-time purchase.
The City's small staff size (11 full-time employees, five software users) means the bid must be sized and priced for a very small municipal finance operation.

The City seeks a cloud-based accounting and financial reporting software system with complete support for initial implementation and ongoing services for all applications the selected vendor provides.

The scope is organized into four tasks: Task 1 Approach & Project Management Plan, Task 2 Software Installation & Implementation, Task 3 Staff Training During Implementation, and Task 4 Ongoing Technical Assistance & Support.

Task 1 requires weekly progress/budget/timeline meetings, a dedicated project manager and technical staff, understanding of the City's auditing and reporting requirements, and a recommended account structure for auditable reporting.

Task 2 requires assistance with financial report writing, import of the prior five years of data for history, and collaboration with Accounting and IT to minimize disruption and downtime during transition.
Task 3 requires personalized training and manuals for power users, at least one recorded training session and manual for all staff, and support for the first 12 months post-implementation.
Task 4 requires automated updates and software change communications, support for annual e-filing such as 1099s and W-2s, and a help desk or ticketing system for support prioritization.
The City's goal is to go live on July 1, 2026, to align with the new fiscal year, with the project starting soon after contract award and negotiation.

Respondents must supply an implementation plan and timeline, implementation and recurring support levels, key implementation personnel, training options by license level (in person, virtual, or recorded), and a client engagement approach including an account manager.

Proposals are scored on four weighted criteria: 45% response to project goals and scope, 25% technical support during implementation and ongoing, 20% fee proposal and implementation schedule, and 10% information, qualifications, and references.
Written questions are due July 31, 2025, with the City's responses posted on www.colfax-ca.gov by August 14, 2025.
Proposals are due August 28, 2025 at 4:00 PM PST, with finalists notified September 11, 2025, virtual finalist interviews (if needed) on September 25, 2025, and contract award by October 22, 2025.

Only qualified proposals meeting the RFP's specifications go to the selection committee, and the City may reject any proposal on fit, form, function, or cost and may select a finalist group for interviews or award without interviews.
The City may ask finalists for additional formal responses or clarification, but price proposals cannot be altered or modified as part of clarification.
Respondents must submit at least three references for similar services with valid email addresses, and failure to provide a valid email may result in rejection.
The City prefers at least one local referral available for an in-person software demonstration, and Tab 1 requires an outline of virtual demo availability to view product capabilities.
The City will consider the extent to which each solution addresses its needs, and non-compliance with any individual requirement may lead the City to reject a proposal in its entirety.

Reimbursable expenses must be capped in the price proposal, as the City will not accept unlimited reimbursable expenses, and Attachment A requires three totals: total price for all services and deliverables, total reimbursable expenses cap, and total price proposal.

Proposals must include one signed original hard copy plus one digital PDF, must not exceed 20 pages (plus 2 pages for the cover letter and 5 for appendices), and must be emailed to accounting@colfax-ca.gov and delivered to Attn: Shanna Stahl, PO Box 702, Colfax, CA 95713 (USPS) or 33 S. Main Street, Colfax, CA 95713 by the deadline; late and FAX submissions are not accepted.

Any additional or modified terms and conditions submitted with a proposal will be rejected and not evaluated, and noncompliance with or attempts to alter that notice are grounds to reject the proposal as nonresponsive; exceptions must instead be raised as questions by July 31, 2025.

Attachment C requires the Respondent to state whether any work will be performed outside the United States, list those locations and the corporate structure of offshore personnel, and give written notice of any relocation abroad; the City will weigh the resulting risks and costs in award.

Attachment D requires certification of stable financial condition, an unqualified latest audit opinion, no outstanding IRS or other government liabilities or liens, current federal and state taxes and withholdings, and no litigation affecting performance, with notice to the Contract Lead within 15 days of any material change.
Attachment E requires proof of insurance including workers compensation and commercial general liability coverage.

Attachment F is a Software Abilities and Requirements Excel spreadsheet that the City provides as a separate document and that must be completed and returned with the submission; Attachment G requires documentation of financial data protection measures and secure access controls.
The City's standard contract with terms and conditions is available upon request but is not included in the RFP, so the bid team must obtain and review it before responding.
The City's fiscal year ends June 30, so a July 1, 2026 go-live coincides with the start of a new fiscal year.
The City's finance operation is very small — 11 full-time employees and five software users — so the project plan is scaled to a single-site, low-headcount implementation.
The City currently runs Fund Balance from Tyler Technologies with Accounts Payable, Accounts Receivable, General Ledger, Payroll, Utility Billing and Business Licensing modules.
The City has five users of its current system.
The City licenses five users today, which is the basis for the proposed license count.
The historical data to be migrated sits in the City's existing Tyler Technologies Fund Balance system.
The City has 11 full-time employees, so training can be delivered to the whole staff in a small number of sessions.
The City's current Accounts Payable module includes 1099 filing, so annual 1099 support is a live obligation rather than a hypothetical one.
The City will not accept unlimited reimbursable expenses, so the proposal carries a stated cap.
The City requires documentation of financial data protection measures and secure access controls as a condition of the submission.
The City's standard contract terms and conditions are not included in the RFP and must be obtained and reviewed before responding.
The City prefers at least one local referral available for an in-person software demonstration.
The City's written questions are due July 31, 2025, with answers posted on the City website by August 14, 2025.

The replacement system is assumed to cover all six modules the City runs today — Accounts Payable, Accounts Receivable, General Ledger, Payroll, Utility Billing and Business Licensing — with no module dropped, and any module the City later chooses to retire is priced as an option rather than assumed out of scope.
Licensing is assumed to be based on the City's current five users, with the proposal quoting a per-user price so additional users can be added without renegotiation.
July 1, 2026 is treated as a firm contractual go-live date, with implementation assumed to begin within four weeks of the October 22, 2025 award date.
The 12 months of post-implementation support is assumed to be included in the base recurring price and to start at go-live, with any extension priced as an annual renewal.

The prior five years of data are assumed to be supplied by the City as an extract from its current Tyler Technologies system, with the vendor responsible for mapping and loading and the City responsible for validating reconciled totals.
The reimbursable expenses cap is assumed to be set by the bidder at a modest fixed amount covering travel and incidental costs, since the RFP states no ceiling.
The total price proposal is assumed to be the total price for all services and deliverables plus the reimbursable expenses cap, and the price proposal is presented on that basis.

The Attachment F and Attachment G software requirements are assumed to match the functional scope described in the RFP narrative, and the completed spreadsheets are returned with the submission and reconciled to the proposal narrative.

The Attachment G data-protection documentation is assumed to be acceptable as a narrative with policy extracts and architecture diagrams, since no named security framework or certification is specified.
Insurance is assumed to be evidenced at the firm's standard limits for workers compensation and commercial general liability, with limits confirmed against the City's contract once obtained.
The certification notification obligation is assumed to be satisfied by notifying both the City and the Contract Lead within 15 days, the shorter of the two stated periods.

The standard City contract for services is assumed to be obtainable on request before the July 31, 2025 question deadline, and any unacceptable terms are raised as questions rather than as proposal exceptions.
The August 28, 2025 submission deadline and September 25, 2025 interview date are assumed to be binding, with any change communicated by written addendum.

Attachment F and G requirements not available before the deadline. The RFP requires the Attachment F software abilities spreadsheet and the Attachment G software application requirements to be completed and returned, but neither document is in the RFP package, and Attachment G is also cited as the source of the data-protection documentation. The bid team cannot confirm the functional scope it is pricing, cannot complete the mandatory spreadsheets, and risks a nonresponsive submission or a price built on the wrong requirement set. Two mandatory submission items (R095, R096) depend on documents the RFP does not include, and the solution's own assumption that Attachment F matches the narrative scope is unverified. Without them the bid cannot be completed as specified.

Standard City contract terms never reviewed before pricing. The General Contract Terms and Conditions and the standard City contract for services are referenced but not included, and the RFP forbids submitting exceptions or modified terms in the proposal. The bidder must accept unknown indemnity, insurance, liability and termination terms as binding, and any term it cannot live with can only be raised as a question before July 31, 2025 or not at all. R036 and R037 make every RFP term enforceable and R023 rejects added or modified terms, while the contract documents are absent from the package. The bidder is committing to unseen obligations.

July 1, 2026 go-live treated as firm but stated only as a goal. The RFP describes July 1, 2026 as the City's goal and never fixes the implementation start date, yet the proposed solution builds the whole schedule backwards from that date and treats it as a contractual milestone. If award slips past October 22, 2025 or the City negotiates for weeks, the implementation window shrinks and the vendor either absorbs overtime or misses the fiscal-year cutover, leaving the City opening a fiscal year on two systems. The solution assumes implementation starts within four weeks of award and that July 1, 2026 is firm, while the RFP leaves both open. A full six-module replacement with five years of migration in roughly eight months is tight even on the assumed start.

Five years of legacy data migration scoped without knowing the data. The solution commits to importing five years of history from the City's Tyler Technologies Fund Balance system, but the RFP does not state the extract format, data quality, volume or who cleanses it. Poor legacy data or an extract the incumbent will not readily provide turns a fixed-fee migration into unplanned reconciliation work and can delay cutover. R104 makes the migration mandatory and the solution prices it as a fixed fee, but the data source and condition are unsettled and the incumbent vendor's cooperation is an assumption, not a fact.

Reimbursable expense cap set by the bidder with no City ceiling. The RFP requires a capped reimbursable expense figure and three related totals but gives no ceiling or basis, and the solution assumes the bidder sets a modest fixed cap and that the total price proposal is the services price plus that cap. If the City reads the cap differently, or if travel to a Sierra Nevada foothills site exceeds the modest allowance, the vendor absorbs the difference or the price is judged non-compliant. R082, R117, R118 and R119 all bear on the pricing presentation and the RFP settles neither the cap level nor how the three totals relate. The solution's assumption is a guess about the City's intent.

Certification notification periods conflict (30 days vs 15 days). R093 requires notice to the City within 30 days of a material change to the certification, while R133 requires notice to the Contract Lead within 15 days of the same change. The solution resolves this by applying the shorter period to both, which is safe on timing but leaves the recipient and the certification's validity period undefined, so a notice sent to the wrong party could still be treated as a breach. The two requirements genuinely conflict and the RFP does not identify the Contract Lead or state how long the certification must remain valid. The solution's workaround addresses timing only.

Insurance limits and endorsements unknown when pricing. Attachment E proof of insurance is mandatory, but the RFP states no coverage limits, additional-insured status or certificate form, and the Attachment E form itself is not in the package. The solution assumes the firm's standard workers compensation and commercial general liability limits will suffice; if the City's contract demands higher limits or additional-insured endorsements, the vendor pays for upgraded coverage or the bid is nonresponsive. R094 makes proof of insurance a submission condition and the coverage is described as 'including, but not limited to', so the required scope is open-ended. The limits are only confirmable once the City's contract is obtained.

Attachment G data-protection evidence may not match an unstated standard. The solution delivers the data-protection and access-control documentation as a narrative with policy extracts and architecture diagrams, on the assumption that no named security framework is required. If the City expects a recognised certification or a prescribed format, the pack needs rework after submission or at acceptance, and the 45%-weighted scope response is weakened. R096 requires documentation of financial data protection and secure access controls but the RFP names no framework or format, and the Attachment G form that would define it is missing. The solution's narrative approach is an assumption.

Module scope and user count not fixed by the RFP. The RFP lists the City's current six modules and five users but never says whether all six must be replaced or whether the five users are the licensed count. The solution assumes all six modules stay in scope and prices five named users with headroom; if the City expects growth capacity or a different licensing basis, the license and implementation price is wrong. R008 and R056 require the response to cover the functional areas and license types, but the RFP leaves the in-scope module list and the licensed user count open. The solution's assumptions are inferences from the current system, not stated requirements.

Twelve months of post-implementation support priced into the base fee. The solution includes the first 12 months of support in the base recurring price and starts it at go-live, but the RFP does not say whether that support is included or a separately priced option, nor when the period begins. If the City expects it priced separately, or expects it to run from acceptance rather than go-live, the fee structure is misaligned and the vendor may give away a year of support. R108 makes 12 months of support mandatory but the RFP leaves its pricing treatment and start point undefined. The solution's choice is an assumption that directly affects the recurring fee.

Proposal page limit and submission mechanics could make the bid nonresponsive. The proposal must be one signed original hard copy plus a digital PDF, emailed and physically received by 4:00 PM on August 28, 2025, within a 20-page limit plus allowances, and the RFP is inconsistent about whether the page limit is mandatory. A bid covering six modules, migration, training, pricing and compliance in that space, delivered to two addresses on the same day, risks being rejected on form rather than merit. R039, R043, R045 and R041 impose hard-copy, email and page constraints, and the RFP does not say whether the PO Box or the street address governs timely receipt. The volume of mandatory content is large relative to the page allowance.

References and local referral requirements may not be met. The RFP requires at least three references for similar municipal accounting implementations with valid email addresses, and prefers a local referral available for an in-person demonstration, but does not define 'similar' or 'local'. If the firm's reference clients cannot be reached or do not match the City's unstated criteria, the proposal may be rejected outright or lose points on the 10% qualifications criterion. R089 and R090 make references mandatory and a bad email a possible rejection ground, while the RFP leaves the qualifying criteria undefined. The solution commits to three references without confirming their availability.
